blocks.text: Probability assigns a number between 0 and 1 to every possible outcome of an uncertain event, 0 meaning impossible and 1 meaning certain. This lesson covers the small set of rules that every valid probability calculation must obey, rules that everything from a coin flip to a language model next-word prediction ultimately rests on.

blocks.alt: Overview of the core probability rules
blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What Probability Measures

A probability is a number between 0 and 1 that quantifies how likely an outcome is, 0 meaning it never happens and 1 meaning it always happens. Everything in between describes a graded degree of likelihood, a probability of 0.7 means the outcome is expected to happen roughly 70 percent of the time under repeated, identical conditions.

Probabilities can describe physical randomness, like a fair coin landing heads, or a model degree of confidence, like a spam filter assigning a 92 percent chance that an email is spam. Both uses follow the exact same mathematical rules covered throughout this lesson.

Probabilities are sometimes expressed as percentages instead of decimals for readability, 70 percent and 0.7 mean exactly the same thing mathematically, and both are used interchangeably throughout this curriculum.
2. Every Outcome Probability Lies Between 0 and 1
No valid probability can be negative or greater than 1. A calculation that produces negative 0.2 or 1.5 as a probability signals a bug somewhere upstream, not an unusual but valid result.

code.content:
import numpy as np
probabilities = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.6])
assert np.all(probabilities >= 0) and np.all(probabilities <= 1)   # a standard sanity check

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A machine learning model that occasionally outputs a raw score of 1.2 for a class before applying softmax is not violating this rule, that raw score is not yet a probability, softmax specifically exists to convert such raw scores into valid, properly bounded probabilities.

blocks.text: 3. All Possible Outcomes Sum to 1

If a list of outcomes covers every possibility with no overlap, their probabilities must add up to exactly 1. A weather forecast giving 30 percent chance of rain must implicitly be giving 70 percent chance of no rain, since those two outcomes are the only possibilities and must sum to 1.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A 6 sided fair die has 6 equally likely outcomes, each assigned probability 1 over 6, and summing all 6 gives exactly 1, confirming every possibility has been accounted for with nothing left over and nothing double counted.

blocks.text: This rule is often used as a quick sanity check on a computed set of probabilities, if they do not sum to 1, something in the calculation or the list of covered outcomes is incomplete or wrong.
4. The Complement Rule

The complement of an event A, written not A, is everything that happens when A does not happen. Since A and not A together cover every possibility with no overlap, P(not A) = 1 minus P(A) always holds exactly.

This rule is often the fastest way to compute a probability that would otherwise require summing many individual cases, calculating the complement of a rare, simple event is frequently far easier than calculating the event itself directly.

A classic use case: computing the probability of at least one success across many independent attempts is usually far easier via the complement, 1 minus the probability every single attempt fails, rather than summing every possible successful combination directly.
5. The Addition Rule

For two events A and B, the probability that at least one of them happens is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) minus P(A and B). Subtracting the overlap term is essential, without it any outcome where both A and B happen would be counted twice.

code.content:
p_a = 0.4     # probability of drawing a red card
p_b = 0.5     # probability of drawing a face card
p_both = 0.1  # probability of drawing a red face card
p_a_or_b = p_a + p_b - p_both
print(p_a_or_b)   # 0.8

blocks.text: Drawing a Venn diagram mentally, or on paper, of the two overlapping event regions is often the fastest way to see exactly why the overlap term needs subtracting, without it the shared middle region gets counted inside both P(A) and P(B) separately.
5.1 When Events Cannot Overlap

When two events are mutually exclusive, meaning they can never both happen at the same time, the overlap term P(A and B) is exactly 0, and the addition rule simplifies to a plain sum, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

code.content:
p_heads = 0.5
p_tails = 0.5
p_heads_or_tails = p_heads + p_tails   # 1.0, no overlap possible on a single flip

blocks.text: 6. The Multiplication Rule

For two independent events, ones that have no influence on each other, the probability both happen together is simply P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B). Independence itself is covered fully in its own lesson later in this module, but the rule is introduced here since it is one of the foundational probability rules.

code.content:
p_heads_first_flip = 0.5
p_heads_second_flip = 0.5
p_both_heads = p_heads_first_flip * p_heads_second_flip
print(p_both_heads)   # 0.25

blocks.text: When events are not independent, this simple multiplication no longer applies directly, the conditional probability lesson immediately ahead covers the more general version of this rule needed in that case.

Multiplying probabilities together for a long chain of independent events shrinks the combined probability quickly, which is why highly specific, multi-step coincidences are usually far less likely than intuition alone might suggest.

The word and in probability language always maps to multiplication for independent events, just as the word or maps to addition, a useful shorthand for translating a plain English probability question into the correct formula.
7. Probability Rules in Code
Simulating probability rules directly with random sampling is a useful way to build confidence in a formula before trusting it analytically, especially while these rules are still new.

code.content:
trials = 100000
results = np.random.rand(trials) < 0.3   # simulate an event with probability 0.3
print(results.mean())   # should land close to 0.3, confirming the theoretical probability

blocks.text: Running the same simulation with more trials narrows the gap between the simulated and theoretical probability, a direct, hands on illustration of the frequentist interpretation of probability covered later in section 12.
8. Common Probability Notation
Reading probability notation fluently makes the rest of this module considerably easier to follow.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Notation","Meaning"],"rows":[["P(A)","the probability that event A happens"],["P(not A), or P(A complement)","the probability that event A does not happen"],["P(A or B)","the probability that A happens, B happens, or both happen"],["P(A and B)","the probability that both A and B happen together"]]}

blocks.text: This same notation extends naturally to conditional probability in the next lesson, written P(A given B), and reading it fluently now makes that extension far easier to absorb.
Some texts write P(A, B) instead of P(A and B), using a comma as shorthand for joint occurrence, worth recognizing since both notations appear interchangeably across papers and textbooks.
9. Probability Rules in AI Practice

A classification model output layer, using softmax, is specifically designed to satisfy the sum-to-1 rule from section 3, every class probability it outputs is guaranteed non negative and the full set always sums to exactly 1, directly enforcing valid probability rules by construction rather than by accident.

items: A language model choosing its next word assigns a probability to every possible word in its vocabulary, and those probabilities are guaranteed to sum to 1 by the softmax function used to produce them.
A spam classifier reporting 85 percent spam and 15 percent not spam is applying the complement rule directly, whether the underlying model explicitly computed it that way or not.
Ensemble models that combine multiple classifiers often need to correctly apply the addition rule when reasoning about the combined probability of at least one model flagging an issue.

blocks.text: Whenever a model output is described as a probability distribution over classes, these same foundational rules are silently being relied upon, non negative values, a full sum of exactly 1, and a well defined complement for any single class.
10. Impossible and Certain Events

An impossible event, such as rolling a 7 on a standard 6 sided die, is always assigned probability exactly 0. A certain event, such as rolling any number between 1 and 6 on that same die, is always assigned probability exactly 1. These two extremes anchor the entire 0 to 1 scale every other probability sits within.

code.content:
p_impossible = 0.0   # rolling a 7 on a 6-sided die
p_certain = 1.0      # rolling a number between 1 and 6

blocks.text: In practice, a model rarely outputs an exact 0 or exact 1 probability, even for outcomes that feel certain or impossible, since most probabilistic models leave a small residual probability everywhere to remain well behaved under updates and avoid dividing by zero in later calculations.
11. Extending the Addition Rule to Three Events

The addition rule from section 5 extends to three events, though the overlap accounting grows more involved, following a pattern called inclusion exclusion, add each individual probability, subtract every pairwise overlap, then add back the overlap shared by all three, which would otherwise have been subtracted out entirely.

code.content:
p_a, p_b, p_c = 0.3, 0.4, 0.2
p_ab, p_ac, p_bc = 0.1, 0.05, 0.08
p_abc = 0.02
p_a_or_b_or_c = p_a + p_b + p_c - p_ab - p_ac - p_bc + p_abc
print(p_a_or_b_or_c)

blocks.text: This pattern of alternating addition and subtraction continues for even more events, though beyond 3 or 4 events it becomes considerably more practical to compute the complement of none of the events happening instead, using the rule from section 4.
12. Two Ways to Interpret Probability

The frequentist interpretation treats probability as a long run frequency, the fraction of times an outcome would occur if an experiment were repeated many times under identical conditions. The Bayesian interpretation instead treats probability as a degree of belief, which can be assigned even to one-time, non-repeatable events, and can be updated as new evidence arrives. The Bayes theorem lesson later in this module builds directly on this second, belief-updating interpretation.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Interpretation","View of probability","Example"],"rows":[["Frequentist","long run frequency over repeated trials","a coin lands heads 50 percent of the time over many flips"],["Bayesian","a degree of belief, updatable with evidence","80 percent confidence a specific email is spam, given its content"]]}

blocks.text: Neither interpretation is universally correct or incorrect, they are simply two different lenses for the same underlying mathematics, and most practicing data scientists move fluidly between both depending on the situation at hand.
13. A Worked Example
A weather model reports a 40 percent chance of rain and a 25 percent chance of high wind, with a 10 percent chance of both happening together. Compute the probability of rain or high wind.

code.content:
p_rain = 0.4
p_wind = 0.25
p_both = 0.10
p_rain_or_wind = p_rain + p_wind - p_both
print(p_rain_or_wind)   # 0.55

blocks.text: Notice that skipping the subtraction of P(rain and wind) here would have overcounted the 10 percent of days where both happen at once, inflating the answer to an incorrect 0.65 instead of the correct 0.55.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to subtract the overlap term in the addition rule, silently double counting outcomes where both events happen.
Applying the simple multiplication rule from section 6 to events that are not actually independent, producing a wrong answer without any obvious warning sign.
Reporting a probability outside the 0 to 1 range, usually the result of an upstream calculation error rather than a legitimately unusual outcome.
Assuming a set of listed probabilities automatically sums to 1 without checking, especially when some possible outcomes may have been left out of the list entirely.

blocks.text: A related trap worth flagging: assuming two events are mutually exclusive just because they seem unrelated at first glance, always confirm they genuinely cannot both happen before dropping the overlap term from the addition rule.
15. Practice: Apply the Rules
A bag contains marbles such that P(red) is 0.3 and P(blue) is 0.45, with red and blue being mutually exclusive colors. Compute P(red or blue) and P(neither red nor blue).

code.content:
p_red = 0.3
p_blue = 0.45
p_red_or_blue = p_red + p_blue   # mutually exclusive, no overlap term needed
p_neither = 1 - p_red_or_blue
print(p_red_or_blue, p_neither)   # 0.75 0.25

blocks.text: Confirm your answer for P(neither red nor blue) also matches directly applying the complement rule from section 4 to the combined red-or-blue probability, both approaches should agree exactly.
Key Takeaway

The Bayesian interpretation from section 12 is the one that carries forward most directly into the rest of this module, Bayes theorem, conditional probability, and much of applied machine learning reasoning treat probability as an updatable belief rather than a fixed, unchanging frequency.

Every valid probability sits between 0 and 1, a full set of covering outcomes always sums to exactly 1, and the addition and multiplication rules combine individual event probabilities correctly as long as overlap and independence are accounted for properly.

These few rules are the foundation every other lesson in this module builds on directly, from conditional probability and Bayes theorem through expectation and variance, all of which assume the rules covered here already hold.

The next lessons in this module, conditional probability and Bayes theorem, build directly on the multiplication rule from section 6, extending it to handle events that do influence each other rather than the independent case covered here.
